purpose: Afatinib is used to treat a certain type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has specific gene changes (mutations) in the EGFR gene. It may also be used for squamous cell lung cancer that has gotten worse after chemotherapy. Your doctor prescribed it because your cancer has certain features that make it likely to respond to this medicine.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells have a faulty protein called EGFR that tells them to grow out of control. Afatinib works by blocking this protein, like putting a lock on a door so the signal to grow cannot get through. This helps slow down or stop the cancer cells from multiplying.
common_side_effects: Diarrhea (very common — drink plenty of fluids), mouth sores or ulcers, skin rash (often acne-like), dry or cracked skin, nail infections around the fingernails or toenails, decreased appetite, nausea, and feeling tired. Diarrhea and rash are the most common and can sometimes be severe, so tell your doctor right away if they are bad.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious diarrhea that can lead to dehydration — contact your doctor immediately if you have more than 3 loose stools per day. Rarely, it can cause serious lung problems (sudden shortness of breath or cough), liver damage, severe skin reactions, eye problems, or heart problems. It can harm an unborn baby, so do not get pregnant while taking it and use reliable birth control. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, as some can affect how afatinib works.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is one 40 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day. It is important to take it on an empty stomach — avoid eating for at least 1 hour before and 2 hours after taking the tablet. Try to take it at the same time each day. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects. Swallow the tablet whole with water.
